packet.headline_seed: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptation
packet.description_seed: The film has won rave reviews from film critics but a translator of Homer's work was less than impressed.

what: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptation

clean_source_blocks.text: Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy. Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie. Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky." "The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."

Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy. Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie. Published in the London Review of Books, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky." "The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."
The film has won rave reviews from film critics but a translator of Homer's work was less than impressed.

Christopher Nolan's “The Odyssey” has found one of its sharpest critics in classicist Emily Wilson, whose acclaimed 2017 translation of Homer's epic was cited by the filmmaker as a key inspiration for the film. In a blistering essay for the London Review of Books titled ‘An Uncomplicated Man,’ Wilson argues that Nolan's adaptation strips away much of what makes the original poem enduring, describing it as visually impressive but intellectually and emotionally hollow.

Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy.

Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie.

Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky."

"The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."

"It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth," Wilson wrote, while also acknowledging that Sir Chriostopher 's work had sparked renewed interest in Homer's classic.

The Odyssey is Sir Christopher Nolan's first film since the Oscar-winning Oppenheimer

"The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted.

"This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves... [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments.

"Nolan... is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful."

But she was left largely disappointed by the three-hour epic

"I had hoped that Nolan's affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters," she wrote.

"But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality... the film's vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants."

Wilson added that her teenagers had "had a good time" seeing the blockbuster at the cinema.

payload.title: Odysseian kääntäjä arvostelee Christopher Nolanin elokuvaa rajusti
payload.summary: Antiikin tutkija Emily Wilson pitää Christopher Nolanin Odysseia-sovitusta näyttävänä mutta sisällöltään onttona. Hänen mukaansa elokuvan käsikirjoitus, henkilöhahmojen motiivit ja kerronnan rakenne jäävät heikoiksi.
payload.content:
Antiikin kirjallisuuden tutkija ja Homeroksen Odysseian kääntäjä Emily Wilson on arvostellut poikkeuksellisen jyrkästi Christopher Nolanin uusinta elokuvaa The Odyssey. Wilsonin vuonna 2017 julkaistu käännös oli Nolanin mainitsemien vaikutteiden joukossa, mutta tutkijan mukaan elokuvasovitus kadottaa suuren osan niistä ominaisuuksista, joiden ansiosta alkuperäinen runoelma on säilyttänyt merkityksensä.

## Käsikirjoitus ja rakenne saavat ankaran tuomion

Wilson julkaisi arvionsa London Review of Books -lehdessä otsikolla An Uncomplicated Man. Hän kuvailee elokuvan kerronnallista rakennetta kikkailevaksi ja kirjoittaa, että häpeäisi, jos olisi itse laatinut vastaavan käsikirjoituksen. Wilsonin mukaan elokuvan kirjoittaminen on kauttaaltaan surkeaa, eikä näyttävä toteutus korvaa tekstin ongelmia.

Tutkijan arvostelu kohdistuu myös henkilöhahmoihin. Hänen mukaansa yhdenkään hahmon teoille tai sanoille ei anneta uskottavia vaikuttimia. Wilson nostaa lisäksi esiin sen, ettei elokuvassa ole seksikohtauksia ja että siinä nähtävä ruoka näyttää hänen mielestään kamalalta. Nämä huomiot ovat osa hänen laajempaa kritiikkiään Nolanin tavasta siirtää Homeroksen maailma valkokankaalle.

Wilsonin asema arvostelijana on erityinen, sillä Nolan on itse viitannut hänen kiitettyyn vuoden 2017 Odysseia-käännökseensä elokuvan keskeisenä vaikutteena. Kääntäjän mukaan sovitus kuitenkin yksinkertaistaa Homeroksen eeposta ja poistaa siitä paljon sellaista, mikä on tehnyt alkuperäisestä teoksesta kestävän.

## Visuaalinen vaikuttavuus ei riitä

Wilson kuvailee elokuvaa visuaalisesti vaikuttavaksi, mutta samalla älyllisesti ja emotionaalisesti ontoksi. Hänen arvionsa mukaan komea ulkoasu ei auta, jos tarinan rakenne tuntuu keinotekoiselta, käsikirjoitus jää heikoksi ja henkilöhahmojen toiminnalta puuttuvat vakuuttavat perusteet. Näin hänen kritiikkinsä ulottuu yksittäisistä kohtauksista koko sovituksen tapaan käsitellä Homeroksen tarinaa.

Jyrkkä arvio poikkeaa selvästi elokuvan saamasta yleisestä vastaanotosta. Nolanin The Odyssey on kerännyt elokuvakriitikoilta runsaasti kiitosta ja menestynyt vahvasti myös lippuluukuilla. Tästä huolimatta yksi elokuvan taustalla mainitun kirjallisen vaikutteen keskeisistä asiantuntijoista katsoo, ettei sovitus tavoita alkuperäisen runoelman älyllistä, emotionaalista ja kerronnallista rikkautta.

Wilsonin vuonna 2017 julkaistu Odysseia-käännös oli yksi Nolanin mainitsemista vaikutteista.

Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy. Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie. Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky." "The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."

The film has won rave reviews from film critics but a translator of Homer's work was less than impressed.

Christopher Nolan's “The Odyssey” has found one of its sharpest critics in classicist Emily Wilson, whose acclaimed 2017 translation of Homer's epic was cited by the filmmaker as a key inspiration for the film. In a blistering essay for the London Review of Books titled ‘An Uncomplicated Man,’ Wilson argues that Nolan's adaptation strips away much of what makes the original poem enduring, describing it as visually impressive but intellectually and emotionally hollow.
